messages.subject: Re: new layer trouble
messages.body_plain:
First, for simplicity, let's say

p <- ggplot(..)  # everything except that third layer

Then, what about

p + geom_line(aes(y=AAA_c,size=factor(order_plot)),color='black',show_guide=F)

Note that (i) I've used show_guide, not show_legend, and (ii) moved
color='black' outside the aes() call.

Ben

messages.subject: ggsave Class Checking Error
messages.body_plain:
I have the same error as previous questions, but my arguments to the function are in the correct order. I have a grob that was made by arrangeGrob and returned from a function and assigned to wholePlot.

> wholePlot # Shows a nice graph.
> class(wholePlot)
[1] "arrange" "gTree"   "grob"    "gDesc"
> ggsave("wholePlot.png", wholePlot)
Error in ggsave("wholePlot.png", wholePlot) :
  plot should be a ggplot2 plot

There's a hack I have seen :
ggsave <- ggplot2::ggsave; body(ggsave) <- body(ggplot2::ggsave)[-2];

This hack was published one year ago. I would have thought it'd already be addressed in a nicer way by the package authors.

messages.body_plain:
Dario,

Yes, this is starting to ring a bell now.

AFAIK, you still cannot do this with any multi-grob object created by gridExtra. You need to do it the old fashion way...

png(filename = "wholePlot.png", width = 6, height = 6, units = "in", res=400)
print(wholePlot)
dev.off()

HTH,
B

messages.subject_clean: ggplot2_gtable Unexpectedly Opens New Graphics Device
messages.body_plain:
The code

load("classesPlot.obj")
requireNamespace("ggplot2")
requireNamespace("grid")
requireNamespace("gridExtra")

classGrob <- ggplot2::ggplot_gtable(ggplot2::ggplot_build(classesPlot))

opens a window with a blank plotting area titled

R Graphics: Device 2 (ACTIVE)

However, the documentation for ggplot_gtable has

Value : a gtable object

> class(classGrob)
[1] "gtable" "grob"   "gDesc"

That's true, but why is there a new device opened as a side effect ? It is not documented and it is unwanted.

Furthermore, when I combine grobs, I see no plot, just an uninformative message.

load("errorPlot.obj")
errorGrob <- ggplot2::ggplot_gtable(ggplot2::ggplot_build(errorPlot))
commonWidth <- grid::unit.pmax(classGrob[["widths"]], errorGrob[["widths"]])
classGrob[["widths"]] <- commonWidth
errorGrob[["widths"]] <- commonWidth

wholePlot <- gridExtra::arrangeGrob(classGrob, errorGrob, nrow = 2, heights = c(1, 4), main = grid::textGrob("Error Comparison", gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = 16), vjust = 1))

> wholePlot # Nothing plotted.
arrange[GRID.arrange.134]
> print(wholePlot) # Nothing plotted.
arrange[GRID.arrange.134]
> dev.off() # It's definitely not being plotted anywhere else.
Error in dev.off() : cannot shut down device 1 (the null device)

Changing arrangeGrob to grid.arrange shows that the plot can be plotted correctly. I use ggplot2_1.0.0, grid_3.1.1, and gridExtra_0.9.1 in R version 3.1.1 (2014-07-10).

messages.subject: Re: Add a second legend for NA values in scale_colour_gradient() or scale_fill_brewer() etc?
messages.subject_clean: Add a second legend for NA values in scale_colour_gradient() or scale_fill_brewer() etc?
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

If you want NA represented in the legend, you can finagle the NA in
miss to become an actual factor level and then set the desired color
for it. Here's the basic idea:

library(ggplot2)

miss1 <- miss        # Copy original vector
# Coerce missing values to be character (=> miss1 is coerced to character)
miss1[is.na <http://is.na>(miss1)] <- as.character("NA")
miss1 <- factor(miss1)    # NA is now a factor level

qplot(mpg, wt, data = mtcars, colour = miss1) +
   scale_colour_manual(values = c(rainbow(5), "grey40")) +
   labs(colour = "Value")

The choice of rainbow(5) for the first five levels is not an inspired
choice, but it illustrates the idea. There are any number of color or
palette choices from which you can choose.

FYI, in ggplot2 there is exactly one mapping to any single aesthetic.
More specifically, you cannot generate two legends or colorbars for
the same aesthetic.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: ddply question
messages.body_plain:
I ran into this problem back in 2010 (Hmisc:summarize masking plyr:summarize) so I've avoided the problem since by using the Commonwealth spelling in plyr. This isn't an uncommon event because a number of R packages depend on Hmisc, so it could easily happen that Hmisc winds up ahead of plyr in the package hierarchy without you noticing it.

The speed with which Hadley responded to my question at the time made me realize this is a plyr FAQ. And as Adam mentioned, this is an issue of function masking which has nothing whatsoever to do with RStudio. If you want to continue using summarize(), the safe way to do it is to prepend the package name so that the evaluator (and you) know which package in which to look for it. Returning to Adam's example,

library(plyr)
library(Hmisc)      # Hmisc ahead of plyr in the package hierarchy
search()

tst <- data.frame(x=rep(c(100, 200), times = c(3, 5)), y=rnorm(8))
ddply(tst, .(x), summarize, y=mean(y))    # Error due to masking of plyr's summarize()
ddply(tst, "x", plyr::summarize, y = mean(y))   # Works

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
If we're working with data frames, one could now switch to the dplyr package for something that I have found cognitively easier to process...

library(dplyr)

tst <- data.frame(x=rep(c(100, 200), times = c(3, 5)), y=rnorm(8))

tst %>% group_by(x) %>% summarize(y=mean(y)) # summarise also works

On Fri, Oct 3, 2014 at 9:27 AM, Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I ran into this problem back in 2010 (Hmisc:summarize masking plyr:summarize) so I've avoided the problem since by using the Commonwealth spelling in plyr. This isn't an uncommon event because a number of R packages depend on Hmisc, so it could easily happen that Hmisc winds up ahead of plyr in the package hierarchy without you noticing it.
>
> The speed with which Hadley responded to my question at the time made me realize this is a plyr FAQ. And as Adam mentioned, this is an issue of function masking which has nothing whatsoever to do with RStudio. If you want to continue using summarize(), the safe way to do it is to prepend the package name so that the evaluator (and you) know which package in which to look for it. > ddply(tst, .(x), summarize, y=mean(y))    # Error due to masking of plyr's summarize()

messages.subject: Re: Misaligned y-axis
messages.body_plain:
Since you evidently have not taken the time to learn what "minimal
reproducible example" (MRE) means, it appears necessary to post it for
you. This comes from Rob Hyndman's blog, slightly edited with edits in
brackets:
http://robjhyndman.com/hyndsight/minimal-reproducible-examples/

##################
"An MRE is intended to repro­duce an error using the small­est amount
of code. It saves pack­age devel­op­ers [and R-helpers on mailing
lists] time in wad­ing through messy code that is not rel­e­vant to
the appar­ent bug.

It should con­sist of a sin­gle R script file that can be run with­out
error. The file should con­tain the following three sections:

* Pack­ages to be loaded.
* [Data.]
* The short­est amount of code that repro­duces the prob­lem.

Please get rid of any­thing that is unnecessary.

Try to use one of the built-in datasets if possible.

But if you need to include some data, then use dput() so the data can
be included as part of the same text file. For exam­ple, if you have a
time series y, it can be included in your code by run­ning dput(y),
copy­ing the out­put [of dput(y)], and then in the text file type y <-
then paste. In most cases, you do not need to include all of your
data, just a small sub­set that will allow the prob­lem to be
reproduced.

If you ran­domly gen­er­ate some data, use set.seed() for reproducibility.

Please spend time adding com­ments so I can under­stand your code quickly."

One further point, mentioned by Hadley in a separate but related post on MREs:
* Please run your code in a fresh R session to make sure it works as
intended before you send it to the mailing list.

################

Re your previous question and provided code, I would guess that the
problem is here:

axis.text.y=element_text(hjust=1.8, vjust=0))

Fiddle with these settings until you get the position you want.
vjust() controls vertical alignment, hjust() controls horizontal
alignment.

################

To reinforce Brandon's remarks and to clarify what Dr. Hyndman
mentioned about dput(), here is a small example to illustrate what
they mean. Run this code chunk:

set.seed(23590)    # for reproducibility of random numbers
DF <- data.frame(gp = gl(3, 3, labels = LETTERS[1:3]),
                  x = rnorm(9))
dput(DF)
str(DF)

dput() returns the structure of an R object in text form. It is useful
in R-help lists because:

(i) R-help related lists are text-based (including this one);
(ii) it faithfully reproduces the exact structure of your R object.

Re point (ii), it signals to a potential helper like me that the
object I copy and paste into a local R session is the same as the one
you sent. This cannot be guaranteed by copy/pasting from the console
to an e-mail as most people do.

Every statement in Dr. Hyndman's post is relevant. Please read and
heed. (And that's a general statement, not just to the OP of this
thread.)

Dennis

g <- g + scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(0, 6000,500), expand=c(0,0))
g

messages.body_plain:
Hi Vivek:

I'm afraid dplyr doesn't absolve you from masking issues, which was the point of the post:

library(dplyr)
library(Hmisc)   # see the startup message

# This produces an error:

tst <- data.frame(x=rep(c(100, 200), times = c(3, 5)), y=rnorm(8))
tst %>% group_by(x) %>% summarize(y=mean(y))

# These work:

tst %>% group_by(x) %>% dplyr::summarize(y = mean(y))
tst %>% group_by(x) %>% summarise(y = mean(y))  # no conflict with Hmisc

Dennis

messages.subject: annotating a facet_wrap output
messages.body_plain:
I am producing multiple graphs using facet_wrap and would like to add contextual information (e.g., timestamps, project ID, etc) as annotations on the periphery of the "page".

Here is an example      of what I am currently producing using the following ggplot statements: :

g2  <- ggplot(r_allv) +
           geom_line(aes(x=variable, y=value),linetype=1, color="grey72", size=3, ) +
           geom_line(aes(x=week, y=value, color=factor(id), size=factor(is_profile)),
                       linetype=1)+
           scale_size_manual(values=c(.3,.75),guide=F)+
           scale_color_manual(values=cols,guide=F)+

messages.subject: Re: annotating a facet_wrap output
messages.body_plain:
Brandon,

Thanks for pointing me to grid ... it provided what I needed. I was able to adapt Alan's use of the "arrangeGrob" function to manage both the title and a footnote, though documentation for using the positioning parameters is essentially non-existent and took some experimentation to find what I wanted.  It is certainly flexible, but the results are awkward and sometimes not predictable when used with  facet_wrap.  This entire area (text and annotation of  graphics ) is probably ripe for some evolutionary development.

Here is the current iteration of my code ... and the result:

 g2  <- ggplot(r_allv) +
                geom_line(aes(x=variable, y=value),linetype=1, color="grey72", size=2 ) +

                geom_line(aes(x=week, y=value, color=factor(id),
                              size=factor(is_profile)),linetype=1)+
                scale_size_manual(values=c(.3,.75),guide=F)+
                scale_color_manual(values=cols,guide=F)+

                labs(x="Weeks", y="Normalized Index")
                gp = gpar(fontface="italic",fontsize=9, col="blue"))
gg  <- (g2+

                 facet_wrap(~label,ncol=nc, scales="free_y") +

                theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 5.5)))
# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# use grid graphics to create objects for title and footnote
title.grob = textGrob(paste(main,collapse=""),
                just=c("center","top"),
                gp=gpar(fontsize=12, fontface="bold",lineheight=.8))
sub.grob = textGrob(paste(Sys.time()),
                x=0, hjust=-.5, vjust=-1.6,
                  gp = gpar(fontface="italic",fontsize=9, col="blue"))
gg  <-  arrangeGrob(gg, main=title.grob, sub = sub.grob)
print(gg)

By the way, do you have any suggestions for controlling the frequency and/or number of  labeled ticks on an x- or y-axis ?  As can be seen in the pdf  above, there are too many to be readable. In particular, when the x variable is a factor [.. which would seem to require a discrete (rather than continuous) definitional variant].

Its easy enough to do in base graphics ... but my attempts to use variants of

      scale_x_discrete(breaks = paste(seq(0,50, by=5))) +

have resulted in elimination of the tick marks and labels altogether.  The continuous variant of this function produces errors indicating incompatible data.

Thanks again

Alex

messages.subject: Re: plotting multiple data frame columns??
messages.body_plain:
The best way to do this in ggplot2 is to structure your data into
'long' (as opposed to 'wide') format. Here's an example:

# Toy data set in 'wide' format - not useful
d_wide <- structure(list(x = c(1, 2), g1 = c(1, 2), g2 = c(3, 4)),
.Names = c("x",
"g1", "g2"), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")
print(d_wide)

# Same data but in 'long' format
d_long <- structure(list(x = c(1, 2, 1, 2), y = c(1, 2, 3, 4), grp =
structure(c(1L,
1L, 2L, 2L), .Label = c("g1", "g2"), class = "factor")), .Names = c("x",
"y", "grp"), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = "data.frame")
print(d_long)

# Now it's easy to plot groups in different colors
ggplot(d_long, aes(x,y,color=grp))+geom_line()

Ben

messages.subject: Re: multiple axes
messages.body_plain:
Hi Lily, this has been addressed many times previously on the
listserv, but basically: ggplot2 doesn't support multiple axes like
this. For the "why" see Hadley's comments at e.g.
http://stackoverflow.com/a/3101876.

It is possible to fake this, but if you really need a dual-axis plot,
I'd recommend either thinking if you can use faceting instead, or
using another graphics package. Or fork ggplot and write the code
yourself... :)

HTH,

Ben

My code is like this:
temp = ggplot()+
 geom_path(data=sourcedata,aes(x=time,y=temperature,color="temperature"))+
  xlab('Time')+ylab('Time at hourly time-step')
show(temp)

Thanks very much for your help.

messages.body_plain:
Bonjour,

Pour faire des diagramme ombrothermique j'utilise ce code :
Pluvio <- aggregate (formula = cbind(Precipitations) ~ Mois, data = db,
FUN= sum) # Données pluviométrie
TM <- aggregate (formula = cbind(TM) ~ Mois,data = db, FUN= mean) #
Données température

grid.newpage()
# Création de 2 graphiques
p1 <- ggplot(TM, aes(x=Mois,y=TM)) +
   geom_line(colour = "red", size = 1.2, linetype = 1) +
   scale_x_continuous (limits = c(1,12), breaks = c(1:12),
                       label=c("Janvier",
"Février","Mars","Avril","Mai","Juin","Juillet","Aout","Septembre","Octobre","Novembre","Décembre"
)) +
   scale_y_continuous (name = "Température en C°",limits = c(0,60),
breaks = c(0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60)) +
   theme_gray()+
   theme(panel.grid.minor.x=element_blank(),
panel.grid.major.x=element_blank())
p1 <- p1 + labs(title = "Diagramme Ombrothermique 2013")
#p1

p2 <- ggplot(Pluvio, aes(x=Mois,y=Precipitations)) +
   geom_bar (aes(fill=Precipitations),stat = "identity", alpha = 0.6) +
   #geom_text(aes(label = Pluvio), colour="Blue") +
   scale_x_continuous ( breaks = c(1:12),
                        label= c("Janvier",
"Février","Mars","Avril","Mai","Juin","Juillet","Aout","Septembre","Octobre","Novembre","Décembre"
)) +
   scale_y_continuous ( limits = c(0,120), breaks = c(0, 20, 40, 60, 80,
100, 120)) +
   theme_gray () %+replace%
   theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = NA, size = 0.1, linetype
= 0.5)) +
   theme(panel.grid.minor.x=element_blank(),
panel.grid.major.x=element_blank())
#p2

# Création d'objet à partir des graphiques
g1 <- ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(p1))
g2 <- ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(p2))

# Fusion des 2 graphiques selon conditions
pp <- c(subset(g1$layout, name == "panel", se = t:r))
g <- gtable_add_grob(g1, g2$grobs[[which(g2$layout$name == "panel")]],
pp$t, pp$l, pp$b, pp$r)

# Réglage des axes
ia <- which(g2$layout$name == "axis-l")
ga <- g2$grobs[[ia]]
ax <- ga$children[[2]]
ax$widths <- rev(ax$widths)
ax$grobs <- rev(ax$grobs)
ax$grobs[[1]]$x <- ax$grobs[[1]]$x - unit(1, "npc") + unit(0.1, "cm")

# Positionnement des graphiques sur les axes
g <- gtable_add_cols(g, g2$widths[g2$layout[ia, ]$l], length(g$widths) - 1)
g <- gtable_add_grob(g, ax, pp$t, length(g$widths) - 1, pp$b)

# Affichage des graphiques
grid.draw(g)

Bonne continuation
Lionel

messages.subject: Units with Two Dimensions (Both npc and mm)
messages.subject_clean: Units with Two Dimensions (Both npc and mm)
messages.body_plain:
Hello, sometimes it is useful to have units with two dimensions, say, a plot margin that is 1/3rd npc, and also, 3 mm (To help align with grid.arrange and aligning in a matrix). The grid unit function can accommodate this:

> require(grid)
> u=unit(.01,'npc')+unit(3,'mm')
> u
[1] 0.01npc+3mm

messages.body_plain:
The single line of Description for plyr::count() (which I assume you
mean as opposed to dplyr::count(), version 0.3+) states:

"Equivalent to as.data.frame(table(x)), but does not include
combinations with zero counts."

Therefore, if you want to include years with zero counts, coerce year
to a factor and apply the table() function to it.

Reproducible example:

year <- factor(sample(1995:2010, 15, replace = TRUE), levels = 1995:2010)
as.data.frame(table(year))

BTW, this is not a ggplot2-related question. It belongs on R-help or
StackOverflow (R tag).

Dennis

Hi:

Your code is not reproducible because I keep getting the same error
every time I try to read your data:

Error in read.table(header = TRUE, text = " \nExperiment         FC
   Pairing\n  'Meister et al.' -2.7476520     yes\n  'Meister et al.'
-0.7436354      yes\n  'Meister et al.' -0.6456768      no\n  'Meister
et al.'  1.1984003      no\n  'Daub et al.' -0.6663321        yes\n
'Daub et al.' -2.3270716        yes\n  'Daub et al.' -0.4944279
no\n  'Daub et al.' -0.6511040        no\n  'hansen et al.' -0.8284366
     yes\n  'hansen et al.' -0.7219839      yes\n  'hansen et al.'
1.1984003      no\n  'hansen et al.' -0.7219839      no") :
  more columns than column names
^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Guess why. (BTW, putting quotes around the paper titles didn't help
any.) Please use dput() to produce a faithful representation of your
data. This is yet another reason why it's a bad idea to copy and paste
data from the R console into a mail message, especially to a
text-based list like this one.

That said, here is a toy example to illustrate how one might do what
you described. I don't expect this to precisely match your
expectations, but you can take the idea and run with it.

DF <- data.frame(gp1 = gl(3, 20, labels = LETTERS[1:3]),
                 gp2 = gl(2, 10, length = 60, labels = letters[1:2]),
                  y = rnorm(60))

# A function to compute medians of y for each factor combination,
# reorganize the output and attach (two-sided) p-values
# for each level of gp1 based on a two independent
# sample t-test

f <- function(d)
{
   require(plyr)
   require(reshape2)
   meds <- ddply(d, .(gp1, gp2), summarise, med = median(y))
   pvals <- daply(d, .(gp1), function(x) t.test(y ~ gp2, data = x)$p.value)
   D <- cbind(dcast(meds, gp1 ~ gp2, value.var = "med"),
                pval = round(pvals, 4))
   names(D)[4] <- "pval"
   D
}

dstat <- f(DF)   # call it on the input data frame DF

# dstat contains the information needed to get the
# median line and p-value annotations per facet

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(DF) +
    geom_boxplot(aes(x = gp2, y = y, fill = gp2)) +
    ylim(-3, 3) +
    geom_segment(data = dstat, aes(x = 1, xend = 2, y = a, yend = b),
                 color = "blue", size = 2) +
    geom_text(data = dstat, aes(x = 1.5, y = 2.5,
                                label = paste("p-value =", pval))) +
    facet_grid(~ gp1)

Note: The values of x in the geom_segment() and geom_text() calls
comes from the numeric codes associated with the levels of gp2: a = 1
and b = 2.

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Here's what Brandon is talking about. Note that I had to remove the
spaces between values in your data because R was reading Strain as a
factor with levels " A" and " B" (note the leading space). That
behavior may be a dplyr artefact, but I don't know for sure.

The following code worked for me:

DF <- read.table(header = TRUE, text = "
Time,Strain,Value
0,A,56
30,A,43
60,A,12
0,B,11
30,B,14
60,B,6", sep = ",")

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

DF %>% spread(Strain, Value) %>%
       mutate(Diff = A - B) %>%
       ggplot(aes(x = Time, y = Diff)) +
         geom_point()

# It's instructive to define

(d <- DF %>% spread(Strain, Value) %>%
       mutate(Diff = A - B))

to see what spread() and mutate() are doing. The spread() function
behaves similarly to reshape2::dcast(), as Brandon noted. The levels
of Strain become the new variable names in the output data set, much
like dcast(). From there, the definition of Diff within mutate() is
straightforward and the result data frame is input as the first [data]
argument of ggplot().

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Use empty facet space and place another plot
messages.subject_clean: Use empty facet space and place another plot
messages.body_plain:
I needed to overlay two plots yesterday and found the library wq, which lets you specify a grid and place plots wherever you want on the grid, including overlapping. You might need to play with it a little to get the effect you want, but here's an example:

##
library(ggplot2)
library(wq)
p1 <- ggplot(iris, aes(x=Sepal.Length, y=Sepal.Width))+
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~Species, ncol=2)

p2 <- ggplot(iris, aes(x=Sepal.Length))+
  geom_bar()

layOut(list(p1, 1:2,1:2), list(p2, 2:2,2:2))
##

Regards,
Bonnie

The problem's not in ggplot, which is just passing things along to the
underlying grid system. I couldn't get this to work using annotate(),
but here's a workaround:

grid::grid.text(expression(bold(mpg == m^-2)), x=0.4, y=0.4)

which at least puts your bolded equation on the plot. Note this is
'invisible' to ggplot, so use pdf() rather than ggsave() to save it.

Ben

messages.subject: RE: How to embolden math expressions
messages.body_plain:
Dear All:

Following code seems can bold the expression:

Bcht=ggplot(wtData, aes(x=Week, y=Weight, color=Group)) +

geom_point(size=3.8) +
scale_color_manual(values=c("red", "blue")) +
geom_smooth(method="lm", aes(fill=Group), alpha=0.1) +
labs(x="Week ", y="Weight (lb)", color="Group")

Bcht+
annotate("text", label="mpg == m^-2", x=8.5, y=267, size=6, family="serif", fontface = "bold")

David

-----Original Message-----
From: Ben Bond-Lamberty [mailto:bpb...@gmail.com]
Sent: Monday, October 20, 2014 1:18 PM
To: Brandon Hurr
Cc: James Henson; ggplot2
Subject: Re: How to embolden math expressions

The problem's not in ggplot, which is just passing things along to the underlying grid system. I couldn't get this to work using annotate(), but here's a workaround:

grid::grid.text(expression(bold(mpg == m^-2)), x=0.4, y=0.4)

which at least puts your bolded equation on the plot. Note this is 'invisible' to ggplot, so use pdf() rather than ggsave() to save it.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: How to use different color value labels in stacked bar chart
messages.subject_clean: How to use different color value labels in stacked bar chart
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

There are a couple of ways you could go:

(1) Define a standalone vector of colors.
(2) Create a factor inside ce containing the vector of colors.

#-----------
library(gcookbook)
library(plyr)
library(ggplot2)

ce <- arrange( cabbage_exp, Date, Cultivar)
ce <- ddply( ce, "Date", transform, label_y = cumsum( Weight))

# (1)
cols <- gl(2, 1, length = 6, labels = c("black", "white"))

ggplot(ce, aes( x = Date, y = Weight, fill = Cultivar)) +
   geom_bar( stat ="identity") +

   geom_text( aes( y = label_y, label = Weight), vjust = 1.5, colour = cols)

# (2)
ce <- mutate(ce, cols = gl(2, 1, length = 6, labels = c("black", "white"))

ggplot(ce, aes( x = Date, y = Weight, fill = Cultivar)) +
   geom_bar( stat ="identity") +

   geom_text( aes( y = label_y, label = Weight, colour = cols), vjust = 1.5)
#-------------

In (2), cols is inside aes() because cols is a column of the input
data frame ce. In (1), it is a standalone vector that is not part of
ce so cannot be 'seen' by aes(); therefore, it must be defined outside
of aes().

Method 2 is safer, especially if this is to be reused. (1) is OK for
one-off use at the command line.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: geom_bar(stat="identity) odd behaviour with positive and negative values
messages.subject_clean: geom_bar(stat="identity) odd behaviour with positive and negative values
messages.body_plain:
Kendra,

This is a pretty confusing example, and it doesn't work
('bac.fung.tuk.color' is undefined). In the future, please provide a
*minimal* reproducible example, stripping away as much complexity as
possible. But I think you're asking two things: (i) why can't you
stack positive and negative bars at the same x position, and (ii) why
do things change with sorting. About the first, take a simpler sample
dataset:

> test <- data.frame(x=c(1,1), y=c(3,-1), z=c('a','b'))
> ggplot(test,aes(x, y, fill=z))+geom_bar(stat='identity', position='dodge')  # this doesn't work as we want

The trick is to split the negative and positive values into different
ggplot layers:

> test_pos <- subset(test, y>=0)
> test_neg <- subset(test, y<0)
> ggplot() +
      geom_bar(data=test_pos, aes(x,y,fill=z), stat='identity') +
      geom_bar(data=test_neg, aes(x,y,fill=z), stat='identity')

As for the second question...I'm not sure what's happening. If you can
provide a simple, minimal, reproducible example, that will make things
easier to diagnose.

Regards,
Ben

that with plot.margin should get you the desired effect, I think, e.g.

> last_plot() + theme(legend.position = c(-0.05, -0.05), plot.margin=unit(c(0.5,0.5,1.5,0.5),"cm"))

Ben

messages.subject_clean: somewhat OT: current world political map in format suitable for map_data()
messages.body_plain:
The maps in library(maps) date to the 1980s, and in particular the
'world' map is laughably out of date in its depiction of eastern
Europe and central Asia.  I can find lots of more up-to-date maps
online (e.g. at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Blank_maps )
but not in any format recognizably related to the format map_data()
expects.

Does anyone know of a source for a _current_ world political map in a
format suitable for map_data(), or a conversion tool?  High resolution
is not necessary, this is probably going to be reproduced at no more
than a couple inches square in a paper.

Thanks,
zw

messages.body_plain:
Ben,

I played with it for a while and I think I've managed to get it there, but it's clipped. I'm not sure how to prevent that clipping...

B

library(ggplot2)
library(gtable)
library(grid)

grid.newpage()

# two plots
p1 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, disp)) + geom_line(colour = "blue") + theme_bw()
p2 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, drat)) + geom_line(colour = "red") + theme_bw() %+replace%
    theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = NA))

# extract gtable
g1 <- ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(p1))
g2 <- ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(p2))

# overlap the panel of 2nd plot on that of 1st plot
pp <- c(subset(g1$layout, name == "panel", se = t:r))
g <- gtable_add_grob(g1, g2$grobs[[which(g2$layout$name == "panel")]], pp$t,
    pp$l, pp$b, pp$l)

# axis tweaks
ia <- which(g2$layout$name == "axis-l")
ga <- g2$grobs[[ia]]
ax <- ga$children[[2]]
ax$widths <- rev(ax$widths)
ax$grobs <- rev(ax$grobs)
ax$grobs[[1]]$x <- ax$grobs[[1]]$x - unit(1, "npc") + unit(0.15, "cm")
g <- gtable_add_cols(g, g2$widths[g2$layout[ia, ]$l], length(g$widths) - 1)
g <- gtable_add_grob(g, ax, pp$t, length(g$widths) - 1, pp$b)

il <- which(g2$layout$name == "ylab")
gl <- g2$grobs[[il]]
gl$x <- gl$x - unit(1, "npc") + unit(0.15, "cm")

g <- gtable_add_cols(g, g2$widths[g2$layout[il, ]$l], length(g$widths) - 1)
g <- gtable_add_grob(g, gl, pp$t, length(g$widths) - 1, pp$b)

# draw it
grid.draw(g)

messages.subject: Re: Using a calculated Vline across plots w facet_grid
messages.subject_clean: Using a calculated Vline across plots w facet_grid
messages.body_plain:
You need to create a data frame that contains the mean of mpg by cyl
and pass that to geom_vline(). Said data frame requires the faceting
variable cyl and the xintercept aesthetic maps to the mean value. I'd
also suggest taking the aesthetic mapping out of ggplot() and place it
in geom_histogram() instead. Something like

library(plyr)
library(ggplot2)

avgmpg <- plyr::ddply(mtcars, .(cyl), summarise, mean_mpg = mean(mpg))

ggplot(mtcars) +
    geom_histogram(aes(x = mpg), fill = "darkorange") +
   geom_vline(data = avgmpg, aes(xintercept = mean_mpg), size = 1.2) +
   facet_wrap(~ cyl)

Dennis

No, ggplot's not going to display the extra y axis space, beyond
what's required for the data. You can see this by typing

g + scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(0, 2000,100))

...and nothing happens. What you probably want is

g + coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0, 800))

Ben

messages.subject: New Package: Plotluck
messages.body_plain:
Hello ggplot2 enthusiasts,

I have created a new R package, "plotluck", based on ggplot2. The idea is to let the user focus on what to plot, not how - it chooses the type of graph (scatter plot, density plot, heat map, etc) automatically, orders factor levels according to the dependent variable, applies log scaling when it seems appropriate, and orders multiple dependency plots based on conditional entropy.

If you are interested, please install the package from my github page:

https://github.com/stefan-schroedl/plotluck

I hope you find it useful. Please let me know any feedback or questions.

Thank you!
- Stefan

p + geom_segment(aes(xend=xend,yend=xend),arrow = arrow(length =
unit(0.30,"cm"), type='closed'))

The cheat here is that 'scaling factor', which should be computed
programatically from the ggplot size scale...but I just tried various
values to find one that looked good. This may or may not work for you.

messages.subject: Re: Plot size
messages.body_plain:
David,
There are a couple of options to control image size.

You can specify the image size in ggsave(), then insert the resulting image, for example:

```{r, echo=FALSE}
...[your code example]
# save with desired dimensions
ggsave(filename = "your_filename.png",width=8,height=5)
library(grid)
# insert saved image
img <- readPNG("your_filename.png")
grid.raster(img)
```
or, specify the image dimensions in the chunk options

```{r, echo=FALSE,fig.height=5,fig.width=8}
...[your code example]
```

You can also specify other chunk options, such as 'dpi' to improve image quality, especially in Word output (I think the default is 75 dpi). The chunk options for figure height/width only work in the pdf and html output, I think. You may need to use the ggsave(), grid.raster() option above if you're output is a Word doc.

Hope this helps.

Kevin

messages.subject: Order of data in plots
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I was wondering if there is a way to control the order my data plots in the graph.

This is a statistical review of groundwater data from wells.  It is plotting the well in the order of their IDs.  ie. MW1B then MW3B then MW4A.....

I would like to have it do MW1B then WES-14-4-93 then ........

Is there a way I can control this??

My data / code is below.

Thank you for your time
David Doyle

library(ggplot2)

MS <- read.table("http://www.doylesdartden.com/R/MS.csv", header=TRUE, sep=",",)

#Sets whic are detections and nondetects
MS$Detections <- ifelse(MS$D_AMMONIA==1, "Detected", "NonDetect")

#does the plot
p <- ggplot(data = MS, aes(x=Year, y=AMMONIA, col=Detections)) +
  geom_point(aes(shape=Detections)) +

  ##sets the colors
  scale_colour_manual(values=c("black","red")) +

  #location of the legend
  theme(legend.position=c("none")) +

  #sets the line color, type and size
  geom_line(colour="black", linetype="dotted", size=0.5) +
  ylab("Ammonia (mg/L)") +
  ##Graph title
  ggtitle("Lower Mudstone Ammonia Time Sereis")

## does the graph using the Well IDs as the different wells.
p + facet_grid(Well ~ .)

messages.body_plain:
On Mon, Oct 27, 2014 at 1:31 PM, Kendra Maas <kendra...@gmail.com> wrote:
> yes, I did figure it out.  But I'm trying to understand the logic behind
> this so I don't spend hours trying to figure out a work around in the
> future.

The logic is simply that fill and color are not the same thing.

guides(col=guide_legend(ncol=2))+

says "make the color guide have two columns". But the plot

geom_bar(data=mtcars, aes(x=factor(cyl), y=wt, fill=factor(gear)),
stat="identity")

doesn't have a color guide (because nothing is mapped to color). It
has a fill guide, because fill is mapped to factor(gear). So you are
presumably looking for

guides(fill=guide_legend(ncol=2))

The difference between color and fill is that (for two dimensional
geoms) fill is the inside color and color is the outside color.

Hope this helps,
Ista

messages.subject: Heatmap question
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am producing a heatmap with z-values roughly ranging from -4.5 to +4.5.  The color scale I want to use goes from “blue” (z-value=-3) to “white” (z-value=0) to “red” (z-value=+3).  I want to force z-values<=-3 to “blue” and z-values>=+3 to “red”.  Any hints on how to achieve that?

Here’s the code I am using as a start, in which z-values outside the [-3, +3] range default to “grey”.

# required package
library(ggplot2)

# data frame
df <- data.frame(x=rep(toupper(letters[1:10]), 5),
                 y=c(array(1,10), array(2,10), array(3,10), array(4,10), array(5,10)),
                 z=runif(50, -4.5, 4.5))

# plot heatmap
p <- ggplot(data=df)

# tile geom
p <- p + geom_tile(aes(x=x, y=y, fill=z))

# set color palette
BtoW <- colorRampPalette(c("blue", "white"))(4)
W <- colorRampPalette(c("white"))(1)
WtoR <- colorRampPalette(c("white", "red"))(4)
colours <- c(BtoW[1:3], W, WtoR[2:4])
breaks <- seq(-3, 3, length.out=7)

# set color of heatmap cells
p <- p + scale_fill_gradientn(colours=colours, limits=c(-3, 3), breaks=breaks, na.value = "grey", guide="colourbar")

# add text to individual cells
p <- p + geom_text(aes(x=x, y=y, label=paste(sprintf("%.2f", z)), size=2), show_guide = FALSE)

Thanks in advance for any help.

Benoit

On Oct 28, 2014, at 17:49, Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi:
>
> (1) I would have gone about the color issue differently. I would have
> plotted all the points, but increased the size and changed the color
> of the significant ones. To that end, you would need an indicator to
> distinguish the significant from non-significant points. In that case,
> you would have two legends: one for year and one for significance.
> (2) To answer your question directly, put color = "red" inside of
> aes(); that will produce a one-element legend with label "red". The
> problem is that you'll likely get an error message since you'd then be
> trying to map the same aesthetic (color) to two different variables,
> and ggplot2 does not allow that.
> (3) I don't see why you're creating legends for size and shape since
> you never mapped a variable to either aesthetic. I do, however, see
> size set to 1 in geom_line().
> (4) The group aesthetic plays no role so you can just eliminate it.
>
> It appears that you were trying to combine the years as lines and the
> red dot together in one legend. You can do this with a bit of effort
> in base graphics with the legend() function, but that won't work in
> ggplot2 by design. I would suggest that you apply my suggestion in (1)
> for the points and map year to linetype, ending up with two legends,
> something like
>
>
> # significance indicator
> DF$sig <- as.factor(!is.na <http://is.na>(DF$V4))
>
> ggplot(DF, aes(x=dist.class.1/1000, y=Moran.correlog)) +

messages.subject: Re: correlogram plot with ggplot
messages.body_plain:
The only way I can think of is to use point shape 21 and then map fill
to the points, which then frees you to map color to the lines,
something like (untested)

... +
   geom_line(aes(linetype = factor(year), color = factor(year)), size = 1) +
   geom_point(aes(size = sig, fill = sig), shape = 21) +
   ... +
   scale_fill_manual(values = c("black", "red")) +   # note change to fill
   scale_size_manual(values = c(2, 5))

The reason for using shape 21 (circle) is that shapes 21-25 allow you
to map fill color to points. You probably need to add color = "year"
and fill = "p < 0.05" to labs() as well.

Dennis

> The logic is simply that fill and color are not the same thing.

> guides(col=guide_legend(ncol=2))+
>
> says "make the color guide have two columns". But the plot
>
> geom_bar(data=mtcars, aes(x=factor(cyl), y=wt, fill=factor(gear)),
> stat="identity")

> doesn't have a color guide (because nothing is mapped to color). It
> has a fill guide, because fill is mapped to factor(gear). So you are
> presumably looking for
>
> guides(fill=guide_legend(ncol=2))
>
>
> The difference between color and fill is that (for two dimensional
> geoms) fill is the inside color and color is the outside color.

> Hope this helps,
